caseStudies.title: The 900-query request
caseStudies.problem: An internal analytics endpoint served revenue and performance dashboards for 800+ brokerages. A single request issued roughly 900 database queries and took about three minutes to return, which made the dashboards the CFO and marketing teams depended on effectively unusable.
approach: Traced the query fan-out to ORM lazy-loading inside nested serializers, where each row triggered its own follow-up reads.
Built a metaclass-based caching layer so models opt into server-side caching declaratively at class definition, instead of every call site remembering to cache.
Batched the reads that genuinely had to hit the database, and added covering indexes for the dominant filter combinations.
caseStudies.tradeoff: Invalidation moved into the model definitions, so a read can be stale inside the TTL window. That is acceptable for analytics and explicitly not used on transactional paths.

caseStudies.title: One identity across 30+ integrations
caseStudies.problem: Authentication was inconsistent across internal services and 30+ partner integrations including Verizon, MoxiWorks, Century 21 and Howard Hanna. There was no shared RBAC model, and each new service re-implemented login its own way.
approach: Stood up a dedicated OAuth2 authentication microservice on Keycloak as the single issuer.
Extended Keycloak through custom SPIs, and patched it at source level where the SPI surface could not express the requirement.
Standardised SSO and role-based access across services, then took the design through internal security review before rollout.
caseStudies.tradeoff: Source-level modification means carrying a patch set across Keycloak upgrades. The diff is documented and the version pinned, so upgrades are deliberate rather than automatic.

caseStudies.title: Cutting payment failures on a lending platform
caseStudies.problem: Three in five payment attempts failed. On a peer-to-peer lending platform each failure is a stalled disbursement or repayment, so the failure rate was a direct business problem rather than a technical annoyance.
approach: Built the PMI gateway interface as a single boundary in front of the payment providers, with strict REST contracts and input validation.
Added an end-to-end encrypted proxy so every financial call was auditable, with tracing through the full request path.
Retuned 10+ Celery background jobs, parallelising work and tuning concurrency to keep investor dashboards near real time.
caseStudies.tradeoff: Routing every payment through one interface concentrates risk in that component, so it carries the strictest validation, tracing and audit logging in the codebase.
